hook.line: Two sentences that differ by one vowel can mean two different searches: one for a place you've seen, one for a place that may not exist. Vale and Tomás keep swapping them, and the landlords keep answering the wrong question.
hook.es: Busco un local que tenga cocina.
hook.en: I'm looking for a place that has a kitchen.

rule:
The two sentences share every word except the verb ending, so the ending does the work.

*Busco el local que tiene cocina.* The place is real and you know it.
*Busco un local que tenga cocina.* Any place like that, if one exists.

A quick test: can you point at it? Yes, ordinary ending (*tiene*, *abre*, *vive*). No, or you're not sure, or you're asking whether it exists, or the answer is *nadie* or *ningún*: wish ending (*tenga*, *abra*, *viva*).

The article helps (*el* leans real, *un* leans open) but it doesn't decide. The verb does.

English has no switch here. *A place that has a kitchen* covers both. In Spanish you must choose, and a question like *¿Hay alguien que…?* almost always takes the wish ending.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the indicative versus subjunctive contrast in relative clauses: indicative for a known antecedent, subjunctive for an unknown or non-existent one.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tiene* or *tenga* and type the whole sentence: *Busco el local que ___ cocina.* (I'm looking for the place that has a kitchen, the one I saw yesterday.)
yourTurn.answer: Busco el local que tiene cocina.
yourTurn.why: You saw it, so it is real and the verb is ordinary: *tiene*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *abre* or *abra* and type the whole sentence: *¿Hay un café que ___ a las cuatro?* (Is there a café that opens at four?)
yourTurn.answer: ¿Hay un café que abra a las cuatro?
yourTurn.why: You're asking whether one exists, so the wish ending: *abra*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: There's a café that opens at six.
yourTurn.answer: Hay un café que abre a las seis.
yourTurn.why: You're stating that it exists, so the ordinary ending: *abre*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Do you know anyone who lives in Santa Marta? (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: ¿Conoces a alguien que viva en Santa Marta?
yourTurn.why: You don't know if such a person exists, so *viva*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I want an apartment that has a balcony. (any one)
yourTurn.answer: Quiero un apartamento que tenga balcón.
yourTurn.why: Any apartment that fits will do, so *tenga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Switch from the known place to any place: *Busco el local que tiene cocina.*
yourTurn.answer: Busco un local que tenga cocina.
yourTurn.why: Changing *el* to *un* and *tiene* to *tenga* turns a known place into any place.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Hernando conoce a un señor que vive en Santa Marta.* Say: Hernando doesn't know anyone who lives in Santa Marta.
yourTurn.answer: Hernando no conoce a nadie que viva en Santa Marta.
yourTurn.why: With *nadie* there is no real person, so *viva*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. You're asking whether anyone does, so the wish ending: *viva*.

pitfalls.wrong: Hernando conoce a un señor que viva en Santa Marta.
pitfalls.right: Hernando conoce a un señor que vive en Santa Marta.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The man exists and Hernando knows him, so the ordinary ending: *vive*.

pitfalls.wrong: Busco el local que tenga cocina.
pitfalls.right: Busco el local que tiene cocina.
pitfalls.why: Almost. If you mean one particular place you know, use the ordinary ending: *tiene*.

pitfalls.wrong: Hay un café que abra a las seis.
pitfalls.right: Hay un café que abre a las seis.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You're saying it exists, so *abre*. Save *abra* for asking if it exists.

personal: Write two lines about a place you know and a place you'd like. Start the first with *Conozco un lugar que…* and the second with *Quiero un lugar que…*.
